title: Give values names
subtitle: Name a value so the next line can find it.
concept: Name a value so the next line can find it.
intuition: Attach an apple-count label to a basket holding 3 apples.
objectives: Updating a name replaces its value
Numbers and text serve different purposes

body.title: Name a number
body.text: apples = 3 associates the name apples with the number 3. Assignment evaluates the right side first, then updates the name on the left. print(apples) reads that value; print("apples") instead displays the literal word.

body.title: Updating a name replaces its value
body.text: In apples = apples + 2, the right side reads the old value 3 and adds 2 to obtain 5. Assignment then makes apples refer to 5. This is an instruction, not a mathematical equation that must hold forever. Follow the variable cards one line at a time.

body.title: Numbers and text serve different purposes
body.text: 3 is a number for arithmetic; "3" is text. Use a number for a count and text for a name. Names are case-sensitive: apples and Apples differ. This book uses lowercase English names and underscores between words, such as apple_count.

formalDefinition.text: Assignment evaluates the right side before updating the left-hand name. A quoted name is literal text.
conditions: Each example runs independently from the beginning. Start with the stated inputs, then change one thing.

derivation.text: Evaluate 3 + 2 on the right, then update apples.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Starting with 3 apples and adding 2, what value will the variable hold?
interactiveVisual.caption: Choose an input and predict the result, then select Next step. The arrow marks the next statement to execute; the side panel shows current variables and output produced so far.
interactiveVisual.followUp: Start with 0 and watch the right side evaluate before assignment.

workedExamples.title: Two more apples
workedExamples.problem: Start with 3 apples, add 2, and display the new total.
steps: Evaluate 3 + 2 on the right, then update apples.

workedExamples.title: A variable or literal text?
workedExamples.problem: Compare apples with and without quotes.
steps: With quotes, display the text literally.

commonMistakes.correction: Quotes produce the word apples. Use print(apples) to read the variable.

commonMistakes.claim: Updating a automatically updates b if b previously received a's value.
commonMistakes.correction: b = a reads the value at that moment. Later assignment of a number to a does not recompute b.

practice.problem: After count = 4, what does print(count) display?
practice.hint: Read the value associated with the name.
Read its old value and add 1.
solution: The right side gives 5; assignment updates the name.

practice.problem: Assign the text Lin to name, then display it.
solution: Use quotes when assigning the text, but not when reading the variable.

practice.problem: After a = 2; b = a; a = 5, what is b?
practice.hint: When b was assigned, a was still 2.
solution: Updating a later does not recompute b.

answer.code:
a = 2
b = a
a = 5
print(a)
print(b)

learningCheck.question: After apples = 3, what does print("apples") display?
feedback: A quoted name is not looked up as a variable.
Correct: the quoted text is displayed as written.
print can display both numbers and text.
